extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political philosophy and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the inherent virtues and vices of simple forms of government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy), the typical cycles of degeneration, and institutional remedies (mixed constitutions, checks, education, emergency magistrates). Useful for assessing constitutional design and safeguards against corruption and factionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent vice in simple governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple form of government contains a natural vice that will cause it to degenerate over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monarchy tends toward tyranny; aristocracy tends toward oligarchy; democracy tends toward rage and violence. This is a natural 'bane' analogous to rust on iron. Expect eventual degeneration unless mitigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitution / checks and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: A government combining the advantages of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy prevents any one branch from swelling beyond its bounds and degenerating into its congenial vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing branches so each is mutually checked restrains innovations and excesses. The author cites Lycurgus and the Romans as models and notes England as a European example. Effective mixtures require a negative (veto) in each branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate assembly for wealthy/landed interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the rich and proud in a separate assembly and bind their hands so they cannot use combined power with popular representatives to destroy equality and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separating the wealthy uses their abilities as a solid check on representatives and the executive while disarming them of the ability to mischief when united with other branches. This reduces the risk that wealth will dominate legislation and government.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's share in government (powers to elect and legislate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant the people a share in government including choosing annual magistrates, confirming and repealing laws, declaring war and making peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valerius argues that giving the people these powers preserves the commonwealth, assures liberty and power, and establishes perpetual union and harmony. However, popular power needs countermeasures to prevent demagogic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's judicial power to try public offenders
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the people to try offenders accused of crimes against the state (sedition, aiming at tyranny, collusion with enemies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrusting the people with such trials increases accountability. The text recommends making transgressions formidable by appointing many inspectors and guards; people trying high offenders serve as a check on elite corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency magistrate / dictator as corrective safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for a temporary, absolute magistrate (dictator) in exceptional circumstances to curb popular excesses or remove corrupted elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valerius suggests that when the people become dangerous, a prudent person created dictator can, within a short fixed period (e.g., six months), exercise absolute power to cut off infected parts of the commonwealth, reform laws, excite virtue, appoint prudent magistrates, and then return to private life without further reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative negatives (vetoes) in each branch
rubrics_metrics.description: Each branch of government needs a negative or veto power to prevent another branch from becoming dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes Rome's lack of equal negatives and stresses that there can be no equal mixture without a negative in each branch. Practical remedies include integrating magistrates into the legislature or creating parallel councils that can check one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional oversight and many inspectors/guards
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint numerous inspectors and guards to make transgressions of the laws formidable and to watch over ambitious officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger, multiple layers of oversight improve the constitution by raising the cost of illegal or corrupt actions and by constraining insolent and ambitious persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as foundation of virtue and good governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of education and laws should be contrived to produce the virtues of fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and justice throughout the city and its citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's model emphasizes early, law-aligned education that forms 'guardians' who defend the constitution. Neglect of education leads to false reasoning, licentiousness, and eventual constitutional decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritocratic selection and correct promotion of rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers and guardians should be chosen and rewarded according to true merit and genius rather than birth or wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes in distinguishing types of genius (golden, silver, brazen, iron) lead to discord; promotion and rewards must reflect genuine ability to preserve the constitution and avoid factional divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent corruption and bribery in popular elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and guard against the natural tendency in popular elections toward entertainments, secret intrigues, and bribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because candidates often have nearly equal merits, ambitious individuals may resort to bribery or popular arts; safeguards (separate assemblies, oversight, or institutional constraints) are necessary to prevent elections from degenerating into corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of landed property to slow degeneracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A balance of landed property among the people reduces the speed with which a polity degenerates into corruption, rage, and violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When property is decisively in the hands of the people, progression to degeneracy is slower, though not prevented; distribution of property is a structural factor in constitutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wealth-based political enfranchisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allocate political power or offices purely by valuation or wealth, since that produces oligarchy and divides the city into rich and poor factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation-based appointment (giving more power to the wealthy) leads to poor governance, two societies within one city, inability to wage war properly, and moral decline; competent persons may be excluded despite superior skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit unnecessary pleasures; cultivate temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Public policy and education should curb unnecessary, indulgent pleasures and cultivate temperance to prevent moral decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unchecked pursuit of luxury and unnecessary pleasures (the 'unnecessary' vs. 'necessary' goods) promotes licentiousness, undermines education and discipline, and contributes to shifts from oligarchy to democracy and onward to tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against excess liberty and anarchy leading to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive liberty and indulgence in democratic equality produce anarchy in private and public life that ultimately fosters tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When families, teachers, and social hierarchies are undermined, citizens become delicate and intolerant of any master; this degeneracy of discipline and law leads from democracy to tyranny unless checked by institutions, education, or corrective magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure representative parity and adequate counterbalancing structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid structural imbalances such as a single magistrate among a powerful senate; ensure that magistrates are integrated into countervailing legislative structures or that parallel councils exist to prevent necessity of dictators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes Rome's arrangement where a single magistrate could not match the senate and suggests either making consuls integral to the legislature or creating another council of two or three hundred representing the people to obviate the need for a dictator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address the specific dangers of oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchic rule, where the rich govern and the poor are excluded, breeds poverty, concealed crime, drones, and weak public spirit which the magistracy must restrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchies tend to create social division, degrade military readiness (because the wealthy are unwilling to finance public service), and conceal thieves and sacrilegious persons; magistrates should use diligence and force to restrain such elements and institutionally prevent oligarchic excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address the specific dangers of democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy's indulgence of liberty and equality can erode law, discipline, and respect for authority, producing social anarchy that paves the way to tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic societies may honor those who imitate subjects or magistrates, flatter youth, free slaves in practice, and equal strangers with citizens — all signs of erosion. Remedies include education, legal restraints, and institutional checks to prevent the slide from liberty into licentiousness and then tyranny.
